title: A warming world
hook: Play 140 years of temperature records and watch the planet turn red, fastest at the top.
notes: NASA GISTEMP v4 (GHCNv4 land stations + ERSSTv5 ocean data, 1200 km smoothing), decadal means of monthly anomalies relative to 1951–1980; the 2020s average runs from January 2020 to September 2026; 2025 is the annual mean. Grey cells have too few early measurements. Averages quoted are area-weighted over cells with data, computed by Orbis. Values are clamped at ±4 °C.

scenes.title: The 1880s
scenes.text: Each cell shows how much warmer (red) or cooler (blue) a decade was than the average of 1951–1980. In the 1880s, where we have records, the world was slightly cooler than that baseline. Press Play.

captions.1880: Records are sparse: grey means no data.
captions.1940: A temporary warm spell in the Arctic.
captions.2020: The 2020s so far: about 1.1 °C above the 1951–1980 average.

scenes.title: The 2020s
scenes.text: Today almost the whole map is red. The 2020s so far have been about 1.1 °C warmer than 1951–1980 on average, and warming over land is faster than over the oceans.

scenes.title: The Arctic leads
scenes.text: The far north is warming fastest. North of 64°N, the 2020s average is nearly 3 °C above the baseline, more than twice the global figure. As snow and sea ice retreat, darker ground and water absorb more sunlight, which warms them further.
A single recent year: 2025 was about 1.2 °C warmer than 1951–1980 over the areas with data. A few cooler patches remain, mostly over the oceans, but they are exceptions.
